analysis.one_liner: Shields car rental and leasing companies from lawsuits for accidents caused by their renters.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred states from holding rental and leasing companies liable for crashes caused by renters, never got a vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Several states hold rental and leasing companies financially responsible for harm caused by people driving their vehicles, even when the company itself did nothing wrong. This bill would have used federal law to override those state rules nationwide, letting rental companies off the hook for their customers' negligent driving. It preserved liability where the company was itself negligent or failed to carry required insurance. The bill was introduced by Sen. John McCain, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never advanced past a subcommittee hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Motor vehicle rental and leasing companies, and their insurers, gain the most: they would no longer be liable for harm caused solely by a renter's or lessee's negligent driving. The bill's own findings argue this would lower rental rates for customers nationwide and remove a barrier that keeps smaller rental firms out of certain state markets.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits states from holding rental or leasing companies liable for harm caused by a renter's negligent operation of the vehicle solely because the company owns it.
States in its findings that the existing state liability laws raise rental prices nationwide and block smaller rental companies from competing in those markets.
Preserves liability where a company was itself negligent or failed to meet state financial responsibility or insurance requirements, so companies still answer for their own conduct.

analysis.who_pays: People injured, or whose property is damaged, by a negligent renter in states with these laws would lose their ability to recover from the rental company, leaving them to rely on whatever insurance the renter personally carried. Those victims are often severely injured with no other financially responsible party to sue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Crash victims in states with these laws

drawbacks.text: Victims of crashes caused by careless renters would lose a path to compensation: the rental company, which chose to put the vehicle on the road, could no longer be held responsible, and the renter personally may be uninsured or judgment-proof.
Federal preemption would strip states of their ability to set their own liability rules, overriding state statutory and common law that courts had applied for years.

Supporters counter that faultless liability raises rental costs for all customers and deters small rental companies from entering those state markets, so consumers pay higher rates even if they never file a claim.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real, if modest, savings to rental companies and possibly renters, but its central effect was to shift the cost of crashes caused by negligent drivers away from companies that profit from renting the vehicles and onto accident victims. It did preserve claims based on a company's own negligence or insurance failures, which limited but did not eliminate the harm to victims.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, held one subcommittee hearing, and never made it to a committee vote or the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain introduced the bill on May 26, 1999, joined by nine cosponsors, all Republicans.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
On September 30, 1999, the Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs held a hearing on the bill.
The full committee never reported the bill and the Senate never voted on it; it died at the end of the 106th Congress in January 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rental and leasing companies were better off because the bill failed to pass only in the sense that nothing changed; the real winners of the bill's death were accident victims in states with these liability laws, who kept their existing right to recover from rental companies. States also retained control over their own liability rules.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and chaired the Senate Commerce Committee, to which it was referred.

for.name: Sens. Ashcroft, Bond, Burns, Gorton, and Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Joined McCain in introducing the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors were Republicans and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Motor vehicle rental and leasing companies
industries.note: The bill would have freed them from state laws making them financially responsible for crashes caused by their renters, saving them insurance and legal costs. The cost falls on crash victims who would lose a source of compensation.
Rental companies carry large insurance policies to cover this liability; removing it would cut those premiums. Crash victims who would have collected under those policies bear the loss.
